title: Design a Recommendation System End-to-End
summary: The canonical 'design a recommender' case study, integrating the Recommender Systems group's algorithms into one end-to-end interview answer.

slides.markdown:
This topic doesn't introduce new algorithms — it's the interview case study that **integrates** everything from the Recommender Systems group (content-based filtering, collaborative filtering, two-tower models, ranking) into one coherent, end-to-end system answer, the way a real interviewer expects you to assemble the pieces under time pressure.

The shape is the same funnel seen in feed and search ranking: candidate generation, then ranking, then business-rule re-ranking — the specific algorithms plugged into each stage are what differ per product.

slides.sectionTitle: Choosing a candidate-generation strategy at scale
slides.markdown:
For a catalog of hundreds of millions of items (see [deep-learning-recommenders](deep-learning-recommenders)), candidate generation usually means a **two-tower model**: precompute item embeddings offline, embed the user once at request time, and retrieve the nearest items via approximate nearest neighbor search.

Most real systems run several candidate sources in parallel and merge them — a collaborative two-tower model, a content-based similarity pool (for newer items with thin collaborative signal), and a simple popularity/trending pool (for cold-start users) — rather than trusting one source to cover every scenario.

The ranking stage takes the merged candidate pool (typically a few hundred items) and scores each with a richer model using user features, item features, and cross-features (this user's affinity for this item's category/brand/creator). The training label is usually a blend of implicit signals — click, add-to-cart, purchase, return-rate — since any single one alone is gameable or incomplete.

This is the stage where most of the actual personalization lift happens — candidate generation only needs to be "plausible," ranking needs to get the *order* right for this specific user.

slides.sectionTitle: Cold-start handling in a full system
slides.markdown:
A complete design has to explicitly answer both cold-start cases, not wave at them:

- **New users** — fall back to popularity/trending, use any onboarding signal (selected categories/interests), and lean on content-based matching until enough interaction history accumulates.
- **New items** — rely on content-based candidate generation (the item's own features) until it accrues enough interactions for collaborative signal to kick in, and consider deliberately boosting new items slightly in ranking to accelerate that data collection.

Stating this explicitly (rather than letting cold start be an afterthought) is one of the clearest signals of a mature answer, since it's exactly where naive designs quietly fail in production.

Before a new recommender fully replaces the current one, it needs to prove itself safely: **A/B tests** compare the new system against the current one on real traffic, measuring the actual business metric (revenue, engagement, retention) rather than trusting offline metrics alone. **Guardrail metrics** (support tickets, unsubscribe rate, complaint rate) run alongside the primary metric to catch regressions the primary metric wouldn't flag.

Rollouts are typically gradual — a small percentage of traffic first, then ramped up — so a bad model change is caught and reverted before it affects the whole user base.

A common and costly mistake: launching a new recommender to 100% of traffic without keeping a **holdout group** (a small slice of users still on the old system, or even a non-personalized baseline) running in parallel. Without that holdout, there's no way to detect a slow regression — the new system might be quietly worse on some guardrail metric, and you'd have nothing to compare against to notice.

A holdout also protects against a subtler failure: a metric that looks stable in absolute terms might actually be *declining relative to what would have happened anyway* — a comparison you can only make if some users never saw the new system at all.

slides.subTitle: Latency budget across the funnel
slides.markdown:
A typical end-to-end budget for a recommendation surface is 100-200ms. Splitting it out: candidate generation (ANN lookup over precomputed embeddings) gets roughly 20-30ms, ranking the merged few-hundred candidates gets 40-60ms, and re-ranking/business rules plus response assembly takes the remainder — leaving headroom for network overhead.

The reason each stage gets an explicit sub-budget, not just a total, is that a slow ranking model can silently eat retrieval's time if nothing enforces the split — production systems typically set hard per-stage timeouts, falling back to a cheaper path (e.g. skip re-ranking, serve cached results) rather than blowing the overall latency SLA.

slides.subTitle: Re-ranking the merged, scored list
slides.markdown:
Pure relevance ranking on a recommendation surface, left unchecked, tends to concentrate on one brand, one category, or a handful of highly similar items — technically high-scoring, but a poor browsing experience and a missed opportunity to surface the catalog's breadth. A re-ranking pass applies explicit rules on top of the scored list: cap items per brand/category in the top N, inject a small quota of exploration items (to keep collecting signal on under-shown items, see [collaborative-filtering-matrix-factorization](collaborative-filtering-matrix-factorization) on popularity bias), and enforce business constraints (in-stock only, no restricted categories for this user's region).

As with feed ranking, these are almost always a deterministic post-processing layer on top of the ML score, not something baked into the ranking model itself — far easier to reason about, tune, and audit.

slides.subTitle: The recommender shapes its own future training data
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Our training data is an unbiased sample of what users actually want, since it's built from real interaction logs."

**Why it's wrong:** users can only click, buy, or watch what the system already chose to show them — so the logs are shaped by *past* recommendations, not by unconstrained user preference. Items the model rarely surfaces get little interaction data regardless of how much users might actually like them, and retraining on those logs reinforces the same exposure pattern: a closing feedback loop that narrows recommendations over time (a form of popularity bias compounding itself).

**Correct model:** deliberately inject some exploration/randomization into what gets shown (even at a small cost to short-term relevance) so the training data keeps some signal on items the current model underexposes, not just a growing echo of its own past choices.
